{{Short description|Definition in differential equations}}
[[File:Kreis-orthog-traj.svg|thumb|Concentric circles with orthogonal trajectories (1. example)]]
[[File:Parabel-orth-traj.svg|thumb|Parabolas with orthogonal trajectories (2. example)]]
In mathematics, an '''orthogonal trajectory''' is a curve which intersects any curve of a given [[pencil (geometry)|pencil]] of (planar) curves ''orthogonally''.

For example, the orthogonal trajectories of a pencil of ''concentric circles'' are the lines through their common center (see diagram).

Suitable methods for the determination of orthogonal trajectories are provided by solving [[differential equation]]s. The standard method establishes a first order [[ordinary differential equation]] and solves it by [[separation of variables]]. Both steps may be difficult or even impossible. In such cases one has to apply numerical methods.

Orthogonal trajectories are used in mathematics, for example as curved coordinate systems (i.e. [[elliptic coordinates]]) and appear in physics as [[electric field]]s and their [[equipotential curve]]s.

If the trajectory intersects the given curves by an arbitrary (but fixed) angle, one gets an '''isogonal trajectory'''.

== Determination of the orthogonal trajectory ==
=== In cartesian coordinates ===
Generally, one assumes that the pencil of curves is given [[Implicit curve|implicitly]] by an equation
:(0) <math>:\ F(x,y,c)=0,\qquad </math> 1. example <math>:\ x^2+y^2-c=0\ ,\qquad</math> 2. example <math>y=cx^2 \ \leftrightarrow \ y-cx^2=0 \ ,</math>
where <math>c</math> is the parameter of the pencil. If the pencil is given ''explicitly'' by an equation <math>y=f(x,c)</math>, one can change the representation into an implicit one: <math>y-f(x,c)=0</math>. For the considerations below, it is supposed that all necessary derivatives do exist.

;Step 1.
[[Implicit differentiation|Differentiating implicit]]ly for <math>x</math> yields
:(1) <math>:\ F_x(x,y,c)+F_y(x,y,c)\;y'=0,\qquad</math> in 1. example <math>:\ 2x+2yy'=0\ ,\qquad </math>  2. example <math>:\ y'-2cx=0\ . </math>
;Step 2.
Now it is assumed that equation (0) can be solved for parameter <math>c</math>, which can thus be eliminated from equation (1). One gets the differential equation of first order
:(2) <math>:\ y'=f(x,y), \qquad </math> in 1. example <math>:\ y'=-\frac{x}{y}\ ,\qquad </math> 2. example <math>:\ y'=2\frac{y}{x} \ ,</math> 
which is fulfilled by the given pencil of curves.
;Step 3.
Because the slope of the orthogonal trajectory at a point <math>(x,y)</math> is the [[perpendicular#Graph of functions|negative multiplicative inverse of the slope]] of the given curve at this point, the orthogonal trajectory satisfies the differential equation of first order 
:(3) <math>: \ y'=-\frac{1}{f(x,y)}\ , \qquad</math>  in 1. example <math>:\ y'=y/x\ , \qquad</math> 2. example <math>:\ y'=-\frac{x}{2y} \ .</math>
;Step 4.
This differential equation can (hopefully) be solved by a suitable method.
<br>
For both examples ''separation of variables'' is suitable. The solutions are: <br>
in example 1, the lines <math>y=mx,\ m\in \R</math> and <br>
in example 2, the [[ellipse]]s <math>x^2+2y^2=d,\ d>0\ .</math>

=== In polar coordinates ===
If the pencil of curves is represented implicitly in ''polar coordinates'' by
:(0p) <math>:\ F(r,\varphi,c)=0</math>
one determines, alike the cartesian case, the parameter free differential equation
:(1p) <math>:\ F_r(r,\varphi,c)+F_\varphi(r,\varphi,c)\;\varphi'=0,\qquad</math> 
:(2p) <math>:\ \varphi'=f(r,\varphi)</math>
of the pencil. The differential equation of the orthogonal trajectories is then (see Redheffer & Port p.&nbsp;65, Heuser, p.&nbsp;120)
:(3p) <math>:\ \varphi'=-\frac{1}{{\color{red}r^2}f(r,\varphi)}\ .</math>
[[File:Cardioid-penc.svg|300px|thumb|Orthogonal cardioids]]
'''Example: [[Cardioid]]s:'''
:(0p) <math>:\ F(r,\varphi,c)=r-c(1+\cos\varphi)=0,\ c>0\ .\ </math> (in diagram: blue)
:(1p) <math>:\ F_r(r,\varphi,c)+F_\varphi(r,\varphi,c)\;\varphi'=1+c\sin\varphi\;\varphi'=0,\qquad</math> 
Elimination of <math>c</math> yields the differential equation of the given pencil:
:(2p) <math>:\ \varphi'=-\frac{1+\cos\varphi}{r\sin\varphi}</math>
Hence the differential equation of the orthogonal trajectories is:
:(3p) <math>:\ \varphi'=\frac{\sin\varphi}{r(1+\cos\varphi)}</math>
After solving this differential equation by ''separation of variables'' one gets
:<math>r=d(1-\cos\varphi)\ ,\ d>0 \ , </math>
which describes the pencil of cardioids (red in diagram), symmetric to the given pencil.

== Isogonal trajectory ==
A curve, which intersects any curve of a given pencil of (planar) curves by a fixed angle <math>\alpha</math> is called '''isogonal trajectory'''.

Between the slope <math>\eta'</math> of an isogonal trajectory and the slope <math>y'</math> of the curve of the pencil at a point <math>(x,y)</math> the following relation holds:
:<math>  \eta'=\frac{y'+\tan(\alpha)}{1-y'\tan(\alpha)}\ .</math>
This relation is due to the formula for [[List of trigonometric identities#Angle sum and difference identities|<math>\tan(\alpha+\beta)</math>]]. For <math>\alpha \rightarrow 90^\circ </math> one gets the condition for the ''orthogonal'' trajectory.

For the determination of the isogonal trajectory one has to adjust the 3. step of the instruction above:
;3. step  (isog. traj.)
The differential equation of the isogonal trajectory is:
*(3i) <math>: \ y'=\frac{f(x,y)+\tan(\alpha)}{1-f(x,y)\; \tan(\alpha)}\ .</math>
[[File:Kreise-isot.svg|250px|thumb|Isogonal trajectories of concentric circles for <math>\alpha=45^\circ</math>]]

For the 1. example (concentric circles) and the angle <math>\alpha=45^\circ</math> one gets <br>
:(3i) <math>: \ y'=\frac{-x/y+1}{1+x/y}\ .</math>
This is a special kind of differential equation, which can be transformed by the substitution <math>z=y/x</math> into a differential equation, that can be solved by [[separation of variables]]. After reversing the substitution one gets the equation of the solution: 
:<math>\arctan\frac{y}{x}+\frac{1}{2}\ln(x^2+y^2)=C\ .</math>
Introducing polar coordinates leads to the simple equation
:<math>C-\varphi=\ln(r)\ ,</math>
which describes [[logarithmic spiral]]s (see diagram).

== Numerical methods ==
In case that the differential equation of the trajectories can not be solved by theoretical methods, one has to solve it numerically, for example by [[Runge–Kutta methods]].
